title: Postdoctoral Researcher in Organizational Psychology
text:
I am a postdoctoral researcher at the TUM School of Management, Technical University of Munich, where I study what drives people at work — and how much of it they are aware of. My research examines implicit and explicit motives and how they shape behavior in negotiations, leadership relationships, personnel decisions, and social networks in organizations. Much of it turns on a single question: when what people consciously want diverges from what non-consciously moves them, what happens to their performance, their decisions, and their wellbeing?
Alongside this substantive work, I develop and apply quantitative methods for organizational research, including latent profile and transition analysis, polynomial regression with response surface analysis, Bayesian mixed models, and agent-based modeling. I completed my PhD at TUM and have held visiting positions at Stony Brook University and Ghent University. My current project, funded through a German Research Foundation application, extends motive research using large language models.
I also work part-time as a data scientist, which keeps the methodological side of my work close to applied problems.

title: Why measure what people don’t know they want
text:
Ask people what motivates them at work and they will tell you something coherent: autonomy, impact, recognition, a fair salary. Those answers are explicit motives, and they are real — they predict the goals people set and the jobs they apply for.
They are also incomplete. Alongside those conscious preferences sits a second system: affective preferences that develop early, operate outside awareness, and predict a different class of outcomes — spontaneous behavior, persistence, and how energizing an activity feels rather than how sensible it seems. The two systems correlate weakly at best. A person can sincerely want a leadership role while their implicit power motive is low, and the mismatch shows up later as fatigue rather than as a change of mind.
That gap is the part of my work I find most interesting. It is not that people misreport their motives; it is that self-report can only reach one of the two systems. Which raises a practical problem: the indirect measures that reach the other one are expensive to score, which is why motive research has stayed small-sample for decades. Whether large language models can change that is the question I am working on now.

Thesis supervision
Since 2019 I have supervised more than 30 master’s theses and 5 bachelor’s theses.
Topics I am glad to supervise include implicit and explicit motives, negotiation behavior, personnel decisions and selection, perceived listening at work, and social networks in organizations, as well as methodological projects in R. If you would like to work on something in this space, e-mail me at cafer.bakac@tum.de with a short description of the question you want to pursue.

Event: Methods workshop, University of Bamberg
Location: University of Bamberg, Germany

title: An Introduction to Latent Profile Analysis Using R
text:
Context
Latent profile analysis groups people by their pattern of scores rather than splitting a sample on one variable at a time. This workshop covered when a person-centered approach is warranted, how to choose the number of profiles without over-fitting, and how to run and report the analysis in R.
